title: Unexpected Results, Rechecking, and Reporting

unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Recognize unexpected vital-sign values and changes from a patient's baseline.
- Recheck unexpected findings using correct technique and troubleshooting.
- Report unexpected results promptly and accurately to the licensed clinician.
- Escalate urgent findings and worsening conditions using the office chain of command.
- Apply the assist-and-escalate framework while staying within the assistant's scope of practice.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of the blood pressure cuff like a car speedometer with a red zone. 185/122 is deep in the red zone, so you stop and get help right away instead of driving on.

### Question 2

A fever is like a smoke alarm going off. 101.2°F means the alarm is ringing, so you tell a grown-up (the nurse or provider) instead of ignoring it.

### Question 3

Your heart is like a drummer keeping a steady beat. Most adults rest between 60 and 100 beats each minute, like a drummer playing at a normal speed.

### Question 4

Breathing is like a slow, steady rhythm. Most grown-ups breathe 12 to 20 times a minute when resting, about one breath every few seconds.

### Question 5

Imagine a report card with two grades. When the two numbers disagree, you use the worse grade. The bottom number (84) is the worse grade here, so the whole score counts as Stage 1.

### Question 6

If a friend's temperature is usually normal but suddenly shows a very high fever, you don't wait a week. You tell an adult right away. A big change from what is normal for that person is a red flag.

### Question 7

Oxygen saturation is like a fuel gauge for the body. If it drops near empty, you tell an adult right away rather than waiting for the tank to run out.

### Question 8

Think of a triage line. The person whose blood pressure is in the red zone AND has chest pain goes to the front of the line, ahead of people with only a mild fever.

### Question 9

A resting heart is like a car engine idling. If it is racing while the car is parked, something might be wrong, so you flag it for the mechanic.

### Question 10

Breathing too fast at rest is like a person panting after no exercise. It is a clue something is off, so you tell the nurse instead of keeping it to yourself.

### Question 11

Weight that jumps quickly is like water suddenly filling a bucket. That extra fluid needs to be checked by the nurse or doctor, not ignored.

### Question 12

A thermometer is like a health thermometer for a house. Too hot is a problem, but so is too cold. Both ends of the gauge need to be reported.

### Question 13

If two scales give different weights, you don't invent a middle number or hide one. You show both and let the expert figure out which is right.

### Question 14

The 'elevated' zone is like a yellow traffic light: a little above normal but not yet in the red zone.

### Question 15

Imagine running up stairs and then checking your breathing right away. You need a few quiet minutes to settle before the number is fair.

### Question 16

A cuff is like a shoe. If the shoe is too small, it squeezes too hard and the number it shows is misleadingly high.

### Question 17

Think of measuring water pressure at the right height. If the gauge is too high or too low, the number is wrong, so you keep it level with the heart.

### Question 18

Measuring blood pressure is like taking a quiet photo. Everyone stays still and quiet so the picture comes out clear, not blurry.

### Question 19

The cuff needs to listen directly to your arm, like a stethoscope against skin, not through a thick winter coat.

### Question 20

Caffeine, a workout, or smoking are like revving an engine before checking it. You let the engine settle first so you get the true number.

### Question 21

If a calculator shows an error, you don't make up an answer. You check what went wrong and try again, or use a backup way to solve it.

### Question 22

If a drummer keeps missing beats, you watch for a whole minute to get the real count instead of guessing from a few seconds.

### Question 23

Breathing is like a butterfly: it acts differently when it knows it is being watched. So you count quietly for a full minute.

### Question 24

A sensor needs good blood flow to work, like a camera needs light. If the finger is cold, warm it up and try again before giving up.

### Question 25

If a scale suddenly says you weigh twice as much, you step off and check again. A surprising temperature deserves the same double-check.

### Question 26

Hot coffee warms your mouth like a warm drink warms your hands. You wait for it to cool back to normal before taking the real temperature.

### Question 27

If the fire alarm keeps ringing after you check it twice, you don't keep testing the alarm. You call for help right away.

### Question 28

Documentation is like keeping both photos of a before-and-after. You show both so the doctor sees the whole story.

### Question 29

Rechecking is like measuring twice before cutting wood. It prevents mistakes, but if the measurement is truly off, you still fix the problem.

### Question 30

The number on the thermometer is one clue, but how the person feels is another. You share both clues with the nurse.

### Question 31

When the smoke alarm goes off, you tell the firefighter, not the person at the front desk. Abnormal numbers go to the nurse or doctor.

### Question 32

Report like a news reporter: give the facts (the number) and what you observed, without adding your own opinion about what it means.

### Question 33

If you see a crack in a dam, you tell someone right away, not at the end of the day. Fast reporting stops small problems from becoming big ones.

### Question 34

If the teacher is busy, you don't sit on an important message for hours. You find the right person to help now.

### Question 35

When someone asks if their number is dangerous, the assistant is like a helpful receptionist who passes the question to the expert rather than guessing.

### Question 36

Good notes are like a recipe: they include the numbers and how it was done, so anyone reading it can understand exactly what happened.

### Question 37

A scoreboard must show the real score, not a nicer one. Medical records work the same way: write the true number.

### Question 38

When the fuel gauge is low AND the engine is sputtering, you pull over and get help. You don't keep driving.

### Question 39

The assistant is like the person who reads the scale; the doctor is the one who decides what the number means for the patient's health.

### Question 40

Reporting is like passing a baton in a relay. You hand it over clearly and make sure the next runner actually has it.

### Question 41

Chest pain that feels crushing is like a fire alarm. You don't finish cleaning the room first; you stay and call for help.

### Question 42

Think of a hospital emergency room. The person whose blood pressure is very high AND has danger signs goes first, ahead of people with normal numbers.

### Question 43

If someone looks like they are about to tip over, you help them sit down right away and call for an adult, not ask them to keep standing.

### Question 44

If someone will not wake up, you don't wait to see what happens. You shout for help and get the emergency team right away.

### Question 45

If you are not sure whether a beeping sound is a real alarm, you still tell an adult rather than ignoring it until something bad happens.

### Question 46

A very high fever plus a racing heart plus confusion is like three alarm bells ringing at once. You get help right away.

### Question 47

The assistant is like the person who spots the emergency and calls 911 while helping keep things calm, not the doctor who performs surgery.

### Question 48

A red warning light still matters even if the engine sounds fine. You tell the mechanic anyway.

### Question 49

When you need help with homework, you ask the teacher, not another student who doesn't have the answer.

### Question 50

The assistant is like a weather reporter who reads the thermometer accurately and tells the expert, not the one who decides to cancel the picnic.

### Question 51

The assistant measures and reports, like a referee who blows the whistle but lets the coach decide the strategy.

### Question 52

You never paint over a crack in a dam to make it look fine. You tell someone about the crack.

### Question 53

The doctor is the team captain who asks you to double-check the score. You are helping the team, not making the final call.

### Question 54

When someone asks a question only the teacher can answer, you politely say the teacher will explain it, instead of guessing.

### Question 55

When you don't know the answer to a safety question, you ask an adult instead of guessing, because guessing can hurt someone.

### Question 56

Washing hands before and after touching someone is like cleaning up before and after cooking, so germs don't travel from one person to the next.

### Question 57

Shared equipment is like a shared cup. You wash it between people so germs don't get passed along.

### Question 58

Standard precautions are like wearing gloves to handle something messy and cleaning up afterward, so no one gets germs on them.

### Question 59

A disposable item is like a paper plate. You use it once and throw it away, not wash and reuse it.

### Question 60

If a spoon falls on a dirty floor, you wash it properly before using it, not just wipe it on your shirt.

### Question 61

Cleaning shared tools between people is like washing a shared toy between kids, so no one catches the other's germs.

### Question 62

If a cup was used by someone with a cold, you wash it before the next person drinks from it, and you don't hide it away.

### Question 63

If you see someone skip an important safety step, you tell a supervisor so it can be fixed, instead of copying it or keeping quiet.

### Question 64

If you write the wrong score on a scoreboard, you fix it with a clear correction, not by scribbling it out so no one can tell.

### Question 65

Writing down a measurement right away is like jotting a phone number as soon as you hear it, before you forget.

### Question 66

If you measure how fast someone ran in the rain, you write down the time AND note that it was raining, so the coach understands.

### Question 67

You can't write down a temperature you never took. You go take it for real and write the true number.

### Question 68

Making up a number on a report is like writing down a test score you didn't earn. It is never okay, even if it seems close.

### Question 69

If you count 19 in a quarter of a minute, there are 4 quarters in a minute, so 19 times 4 equals 76.

### Question 70

Thirty seconds is half a minute, so you double the number: 9 doubled is 18.

### Question 71

If you are double-checking something, you say 'let me just make sure this is right' in a calm voice, instead of scaring someone.

### Question 72

When someone gets scared by a number, you stay calm, double-check it the right way, and let the doctor explain what it really means.

### Question 73

Asking open questions is like asking 'how do you feel?' instead of 'you feel dizzy, right?' so you get the true answer.

### Question 74

Privacy is like closing the door when you change clothes. Some things stay private, and so do a patient's numbers.

### Question 75

Three steps going up a staircase matter more than any single step. The assistant points out that the numbers keep climbing.

### Question 76

If the scale at home and the scale at the doctor's office disagree, you write down both and let the expert figure out why.

### Question 77

If a measurement seems wrong, you measure again the right way instead of erasing the number or changing the ruler.

### Question 78

If your resting heartbeat usually sounds slow and steady but suddenly races for no reason, that is a change worth telling the doctor about.

### Question 79

An unexpected result is like a test answer that doesn't match the answer key. It stands out and needs a second look.

### Question 80

Sitting with legs crossed squeezes things a little, like pinching a hose, which can make the number read higher than it really is.

### Question 81

A full bladder is like a little extra pressure in the system, so emptying it first gives a truer reading.

### Question 82

If you don't know how to use a tool, you read the instructions or ask someone to show you, instead of pretending.

### Question 83

If a timer beeps an error instead of showing a time, you fix the setup and try again, not write down 'error' as the time.

### Question 84

To recount, you put your fingers in the right spot and count carefully, like re-measuring with the ruler lined up correctly.

### Question 85

Your thumb has its own heartbeat, so you use your other fingers instead, like using a clean ruler instead of one with extra marks.

### Question 86

A breath is a full 'in and out,' like one complete wave going up and back down, not two separate things.

### Question 87

If someone is dizzy from low blood pressure, you help them sit or lie down safely and get help, not ask them to stand or walk.

### Question 88

Rechecking is like looking twice before you cross the street: it makes you more sure, but it doesn't make the cars disappear.

### Question 89

If the situation you reported gets worse, you call for help again, just like yelling louder when the fire grows.
